items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Understanding the interplay between climate change and ecology is crucial when attempting to reconstruct the evolutionary history of species, as well as predicting how modern species may fare in light of current anthropogenic climate change and habitat destruction. Here we use dental microwear texture analysis (DMTA) to infer the foraging ecologies of three lineages of early ungulates (the phenacodontids
                    <jats:italic>Copecion</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>Ectocion</jats:italic>
                    and the early perissodactyl
                    <jats:italic>Sifrhippus</jats:italic>
                    ) across the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM) in the Bighorn Basin of western North America. The PETM was a period of rapid warming and aridification 56 million years ago that resulted in considerable evolutionary changes within these lineages, including phylogenetic dwarfing. Our results interpret both lineages of phenacodontid as frugivorous “mixed feeders” that likely incorporated a large diversity of plant species and tissues, while
                    <jats:italic>Sifrhippus</jats:italic>
                    shows strong evidence of frugivory. This is further supported by greater complexity and lesser scale of maximum complexity in both species of
                    <jats:italic>Sifrhippus</jats:italic>
                    compared to the co‐occurring species of phenacodontids. Notably, only minor changes in dental microwear across the PETM were recovered, limited to textural fill volume in
                    <jats:italic>Ectocion</jats:italic>
                    . These data show that dietary ecology was mostly unchanged within these lineages during the PETM, despite considerable floral turnover and competition from immigrant species. The results of our study detail how herbivorous mammals adapt to intensive climatic and environmental disruptions, hinting at possible responses of modern fauna to present and future anthropogenic climatic and environmental breakdown.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Stable isotope analysis of sequential samples of ancient sheep and goat tooth enamel is used to investigate feeding, breeding, and mobility strategies at Neolithic villages on the Dalmatian Coast of Croatia. δ
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C values demonstrate clear enrichment of caprine diet in
                    <jats:sup>13</jats:sup>
                    C from the Early (
                    <jats:italic>c</jats:italic>
                    . 8.1–7.5 kya cal.
                    <jats:sc>BP</jats:sc>
                    ) to the Middle Neolithic (7.5–7.0 kya cal.
                    <jats:sc>BP</jats:sc>
                    ). The elevated carbon isotope ratios are consistent with a diet consisting of terrestrial C
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    plants from arid environments, potentially supplemented by marine or wetland vegetation during the summer. δ
                    <jats:sup>18</jats:sup>
                    O values are used to model season of birth. The results suggest early examples of autumnal lambing and multiple birthing seasons were practiced by Middle Neolithic (Danilo) herders as early as 7.5 kya cal. BP. Analysis of seasonal signals in intra‐tooth carbon and oxygen isotope sequences suggests foddering was less important during the Middle Neolithic, whereas Early Neolithic (Impresso) herders routinely foddered during winter months, likely in response to seasonally dry conditions between 8.0 and 7.5 ky cal.
                    <jats:sc>BP</jats:sc>
                    . Additionally, the data provide evidence consistent with small‐scale vertical transhumance as early as the Impresso period. The results are discussed in the context of an increasing emphasis on dairying and a shift in the seasonal allocation of labor during the Middle Neolithic.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ground‐penetrating radar (GPR) surveys conducted during the 2024 and 2025 field seasons at the Sanctuary of Poseidon in Isthmia, Greece, investigated unresolved questions concerning the spatial organisation, circulation routes and hydraulic and bathing infrastructure of this major Panhellenic sanctuary. Eighteen individually georeferenced survey grids were acquired across the Roman Bath complex, the East Field, the ground immediately south and east of the East Field, the interior of the Late Roman–Byzantine fortress, and several peripheral zones west of the temenos, and were integrated with archival research and targeted excavation. Rectilinear anomaly networks in the East Field indicate the continuation of buried architectural remains beyond the excavated limits, while survey within the fortress interior reveals a largely open subsurface with only sparse discrete reflectors. Most significantly, GPR anomalies associated with Roman‐period bathing infrastructure were tested through excavation in 2025, confirming a previously unknown heated bathing structure near the Northeast Gate and refining the reconstruction of an earlier bath complex north of the main Roman Bath. Taken together, the results bear on three broader questions about Isthmia: the physical correlates of the attested second‐century AD building programme, the spatial logic of a Panhellenic sanctuary as against the orthogonally planned Peloponnesian cities investigated by comparable survey, and the character of occupation within the Byzantine fortification. The study demonstrates the value of iterative, multi‐season GPR survey integrated with targeted excavation and precise Global navigation satellite system (GNSS)‐based georeferencing at complex, long‐lived sites.</jats:p>
authors: Michael Arvanitis, Jon Frey, Lita Gregory, Morgan Manuszak
